summary: This document describes extensions to OSPF Traffic Engineering for carrying link performance information, such as propagation delay, which matters in networks like financial data feeds where path choice depends on it. Routers can then pick paths using these measures.

plainLanguage.summary: Routers normally choose a path by counting hops. In some networks the operator also cares how fast each link is, for example when carrying market data. This document adds fields to the OSPF traffic engineering advertisements so routers can publish link delay, loss and bandwidth, and so other equipment can choose paths on those values.

what is the anomalous bit in ospf te
how does ospf advertise link bandwidth and loss
subtitle: New OSPF sub-TLVs that let routers share how fast each link is, so paths can be chosen on speed as well as on hop count.

tldr.problem: In some networks, such as financial information networks, link performance such as propagation delay matters as much to path selection as other metrics. OSPF TE had no scalable way to distribute it.
tldr.mechanism: Seven new sub-TLVs of the OSPF TE Link TLV carry delay, min and max delay, delay variation, loss, and residual, available and utilized bandwidth. An Anomalous bit flags threshold violations, and thresholds and timers limit how often values are flooded.
tldr.outcome: Other components can use the distributed data for path selection. Measuring the values and acting on them are outside the scope of the RFC.

today: RFC 7471 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2015. The unit metadata shows that it is not obsoleted or updated by any RFC and that it updates none.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
In certain networks, such as, but not limited to, financial information networks such as stock market data providers, network performance information such as link propagation delay is becoming as critical to data path selection as other metrics. Using metrics such as hop count or cost as routing metrics is becoming only tangentially important. It would be beneficial to make path selection decisions based on network performance information in a cost-effective and scalable way.

This document describes extensions to OSPFv2 and OSPFv3 TE, called OSPF TE Metric Extensions, that can be used to distribute network performance information: link propagation delay, delay variation, link loss, residual bandwidth, available bandwidth and utilized bandwidth.

The data distributed by OSPF TE Metric Extensions is meant to be used as part of the operation of the routing protocol, for example by replacing cost with link propagation delay or considering bandwidth as well as cost, by enhancing Constrained Shortest Path First, or for use by a Path Computation Element or an Application-Layer Traffic Optimization server. With respect to constrained shortest path first, the data can be used to set up, fail over and fail back data paths using protocols such as RSVP-TE.

The mechanisms described in this document only distribute network performance information. The methods for measuring that information, or acting on it once it is distributed, are outside the scope of the document. Any measurement of link propagation delay SHOULD NOT vary significantly based upon the offered traffic load and so SHOULD NOT include queuing delays. For a forwarding adjacency, care must be taken that the measurement of link propagation delay avoids significant queuing delay, which can be accomplished in a variety of ways, for example measuring with a traffic class that experiences minimal queuing, or summing the measured link propagation delay of the links on the path.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers normally choose a path by counting hops. This document lets them publish how fast and how reliable each link is, so a path can be chosen on speed as well as on hop count.

sections.title: The New Sub-TLVs
sections.content:
The document defines new OSPF TE sub-TLVs used to distribute network performance information, building on the extensions provided by OSPFv2 TE and OSPFv3 TE. OSPFv2 TE Link State Advertisements are opaque LSAs with area flooding scope, while OSPFv3 Intra-Area-TE-LSAs have their own LSA type, also with area flooding scope. Both consist of a single TLV with one or more nested sub-TLVs. The Link TLV is common to both and describes the characteristics of a link between OSPF neighbours.

Seven sub-TLVs are added to the Link TLV: type 27 for Unidirectional Link Delay, 28 for Min/Max Unidirectional Link Delay, 29 for Unidirectional Delay Variation, 30 for Unidirectional Link Loss, 31 for Unidirectional Residual Bandwidth, 32 for Unidirectional Available Bandwidth, and 33 for Unidirectional Utilized Bandwidth. IANA has registered one new type code for each.

Many, but not all, of the sub-TLVs include a bit called the Anomalous, or A, bit. When the A bit is clear, or when the sub-TLV has no A bit, the sub-TLV describes steady state link performance, which could be used to construct a steady state performance topology for initial tunnel path computation, or to verify alternative failover paths. When network performance violates configurable link-local thresholds, a sub-TLV with the A bit set is advertised, so the receiving node can decide whether to move traffic to a backup path or calculate an entirely new path. From an MPLS perspective, the intent of the A bit is to let an ingress node work out whether the link referenced in the sub-TLV affects any of its LSPs, then whether those LSPs still meet their end-to-end performance objectives, and then conceivably move the affected traffic to a pre-established protection LSP or establish a new one and place the traffic in it.

If link performance then improves beyond a configurable minimum value, the reuse threshold, that sub-TLV can be re-advertised with the Anomalous bit cleared, and the receiving node can then do whatever re-optimization or failback it wishes, including nothing. The A bit was intentionally omitted from some sub-TLVs to help mitigate oscillations.

Link delay, delay variation and link loss MUST be encoded as integers. Consistent with the existing OSPF TE specifications, residual, available and utilized bandwidth MUST be encoded in IEEE single precision floating point. Link delay and delay variation MUST be in units of microseconds, link loss MUST be a percentage, and bandwidth MUST be in units of bytes per second. All values, except residual bandwidth, MUST be calculated as rolling averages over a configurable period of time.
sections.plainLanguage: Each new field sits inside the part of the OSPF advertisement that describes one link. A single extra bit marks a link that is not behaving normally, so the receiver knows the number is an exception rather than the usual value.

sections.title: Delay, Variation and Loss Sub-TLVs
sections.content:
The Unidirectional Link Delay sub-TLV, type 27 with length 4, advertises the average link delay between two directly connected OSPF neighbours. The delay advertised MUST be the delay from the advertising node to its neighbour, that is, the forward path delay. The value part carries an Anomalous bit, a reserved field that MUST be set to 0 when sent and MUST be ignored when received, and a 24-bit Delay field holding the average link delay over a configurable interval in microseconds, encoded as an integer. The A bit is set when the measured value exceeds its configured maximum threshold and cleared when it falls below its configured reuse threshold. When the delay field is set to the maximum value 16,777,215, which is 16.777215 seconds, the delay is at least that value and it may be larger.

The Min/Max Unidirectional Link Delay sub-TLV, type 28 with length 8, advertises the minimum and maximum delay values between two directly connected OSPF neighbours, again the forward path delay. It carries an A bit, two reserved fields, and two 24-bit fields, Min Delay and Max Delay, each holding a measured value in microseconds over a configurable interval. The A bit is set when one or more measured values exceed a configured maximum threshold and cleared when the measured value falls below its configured reuse threshold. Implementations MAY also permit an offset value in microseconds to be added to the measured delay value, to advertise operator specific delay constraints. It is possible for the min delay and the max delay to be the same value.

The Unidirectional Delay Variation sub-TLV, type 29 with length 4, advertises the average link delay variation between two directly connected OSPF neighbours, again the forward path delay variation. It has a reserved field and a 24-bit Delay Variation field in microseconds. This sub-TLV has no A bit. A value of 0 means the variation has not been measured, and the maximum value 16,777,215 means the variation is at least that value.

The Unidirectional Link Loss sub-TLV, type 30 with length 4, advertises the loss as a packet percentage between two directly connected OSPF neighbours, again the forward path loss. Its 24-bit Link Loss field carries the packet loss as a percentage of the total traffic sent over a configurable interval. The basic unit is 0.000003%, so that the value 2^24 minus 2 is 50.331642%, the highest packet loss percentage that can be expressed. The assumption is that precision matters more on high speed links than the ability to advertise loss rates above this, and that high speed links with over 50% loss are unusable. Measured values larger than the field maximum SHOULD be encoded as the maximum value.
sections.plainLanguage: Delay, how much the delay varies, and what fraction of packets are lost each fit in 24 bits. The largest delay that can be written is 16.777215 seconds, and the largest loss is 50.331642%.

sections.title: Bandwidth Sub-TLVs
sections.content:
The Unidirectional Residual Bandwidth sub-TLV, type 31 with length 4, carries the residual bandwidth on a link, forwarding adjacency or bundled link in IEEE floating point format with units of bytes per second, and MUST be the residual bandwidth from the advertising node to its neighbour. For a link or forwarding adjacency, residual bandwidth is Maximum Bandwidth minus the bandwidth currently allocated to RSVP-TE LSPs. For a bundled link, it is the sum of the component link residual bandwidths. The calculation differs from Unreserved Bandwidth: residual bandwidth subtracts tunnel reservations from Maximum Bandwidth, the link capacity, and gives an aggregated remainder across priorities, while unreserved bandwidth is subtracted from the Maximum Reservable Bandwidth and gives per-priority remainders. The two can be used concurrently, each with its own use case, for example residual bandwidth for Weighted ECMP and unreserved bandwidth for call admission control.

The Unidirectional Available Bandwidth sub-TLV, type 32 with length 4, carries the available bandwidth on a link, forwarding adjacency or bundled link in IEEE floating point format with units of bytes per second. For a link or forwarding adjacency, available bandwidth is residual bandwidth minus the measured bandwidth used for the actual forwarding of non-RSVP-TE LSP packets. For a bundled link, it is the sum of the component link available bandwidths.

The Unidirectional Utilized Bandwidth sub-TLV, type 33 with length 4, carries the bandwidth utilization on a link, forwarding adjacency or bundled link in IEEE floating-point format with units of bytes per second. For a link or forwarding adjacency, it represents the actual utilization of the link as measured by the advertising node. For a bundled link, it is the sum of the component link bandwidth utilizations.
sections.plainLanguage: Three kinds of bandwidth are published: what is left after tunnel reservations, what is left after ordinary traffic is counted too, and how much the link is actually carrying right now.

sections.title: Announcement Thresholds and Filters
sections.content:
The values advertised in all sub-TLVs, except min/max delay and residual bandwidth, MUST represent an average over a period, or be obtained by a filter that is reasonably representative of an average; a rolling average is one such filter. Min and max delay MAY be the lowest and highest measured values over a measurement interval, or MAY use a filter or other technique to obtain a reasonable representation with compensation for outliers. The measurement interval, any filter coefficients and any advertisement intervals MUST be configurable for each sub-TLV.

Implementations SHOULD provide, for each sub-TLV, configurable accelerated advertisement thresholds. The advertisement is made immediately when the measured parameter falls outside a configured upper bound, or a lower bound for the min delay metric only, and the advertised sub-TLV is not already outside that bound, or when the difference between the last advertised value and the current measured value exceeds a configured threshold. For the sub-TLVs that include an A bit, except min/max delay, an additional threshold SHOULD be included corresponding to the threshold at which the performance is considered anomalous, and sub-TLVs with the A bit are sent. The A bit is cleared when the sub-TLV's performance has been below, or re-crosses, this threshold for an advertisement interval, to permit fail back.

To prevent oscillations, only the high threshold or the low threshold, but not both, may be used to trigger any given sub-TLV that supports both. Once outside the bounds of the threshold, any re-advertisement of a measurement within the bounds would remain governed solely by the measurement interval for that sub-TLV.
sections.plainLanguage: Publishing a new number on every small change would flood the network, so values are averaged and only re-sent when they change enough. Two thresholds are used, one to raise the alarm bit and one to clear it again.

sections.title: Periodicity, Enabling and Compatibility
sections.content:
The configurable mechanisms bound the number of re-advertisements, but instability might occur in very large networks if measurement intervals are set low enough to overwhelm the processing of flooded information at some of the routers in the topology, so care should be taken in setting these values. The default measurement interval for all sub-TLVs should be 30 seconds. Announcements must also be able to be throttled using configurable inter-update throttle timers. The minimum announcement periodicity is 1 announcement per second, and the default value should be 120 seconds. Implementations should not permit the inter-update timer to be lower than the measurement interval.

It is recommended that any underlying performance measurement mechanisms not include significant buffer delay, significant buffer induced delay variation, or significant loss due to buffer overflow or due to active queue management. Implementations MUST make it possible to individually enable or disable the advertisement of each sub-TLV. Implementations SHOULD permit the static configuration or manual override of dynamic measurements for each sub-TLV, to simplify migration and to mitigate scenarios where dynamic measurements are not possible.

As in the OSPFv2 TE specification, an unrecognized TLV should be silently ignored: it should not be processed, but it should be included in LSAs sent to OSPF neighbours.
sections.plainLanguage: By default a router measures every 30 seconds and re-advertises every 120 seconds at most, and no more than once a second. Each field can be switched on or off separately, and a fixed value can be set by hand where measuring is not possible.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The document does not introduce security issues beyond those discussed in the OSPFv2 TE specification. OSPFv2 HMAC-SHA provides additional protection for OSPFv2. OSPFv3 IPsec and the OSPFv3 Authentication Trailer provide additional protection for OSPFv3. OSPF Keying and Authentication for Routing Protocols provides an analysis of OSPFv2 and OSPFv3 routing security, and OSPFv2 Security Extensions provides extensions designed to address the identified gaps in OSPFv2.
sections.plainLanguage: The new fields carry no new risk beyond the rest of OSPF, so the usual OSPF authentication mechanisms apply.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content: IANA maintains the registry for the Link TLV sub-TLVs. For OSPF TE Metric Extensions, one new type code for each sub-TLV defined in this document has been registered: 27 for Unidirectional Link Delay, 28 for Min/Max Unidirectional Link Delay, 29 for Unidirectional Delay Variation, 30 for Unidirectional Link Loss, 31 for Unidirectional Residual Bandwidth, 32 for Unidirectional Available Bandwidth, and 33 for Unidirectional Utilized Bandwidth.
sections.plainLanguage: IANA assigned each of the seven new fields its own number, from 27 to 33.

viz.caption: THE SEVEN NEW LINK SUB-TLVs (RFC 7471, SECTION 3)

items.label: Min/Max Unidirectional Link Delay
items.desc: Lowest and highest delay in microseconds. Length 8.

items.label: Unidirectional Delay Variation
items.desc: Average delay variation in microseconds. Length 4.

items.label: Unidirectional Link Loss
items.desc: Packet loss as a percentage. Length 4.

items.label: Unidirectional Residual Bandwidth
items.desc: Bandwidth left after RSVP-TE reservations. Length 4.

items.label: Unidirectional Available Bandwidth
items.desc: Residual bandwidth minus the traffic actually forwarded. Length 4.

items.label: Unidirectional Utilized Bandwidth
items.desc: Actual measured utilization of the link. Length 4.

viz.caption: THE UNIDIRECTIONAL LINK DELAY SUB-TLV (RFC 7471, SECTION 4.1)

fields.name: Type
fields.desc: Identifies the sub-TLV. This one has a type of 27.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Length of the sub-TLV. This one has a length of 4.

fields.name: A
fields.desc: The Anomalous bit. Set when the measured value exceeds its configured maximum threshold.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: Reserved for future use. MUST be set to 0 when sent and ignored when received.

fields.name: Delay
fields.desc: Average link delay over a configurable interval, in microseconds, as an integer. The maximum value is 16,777,215.

viz.caption: THE THREE BANDWIDTH MEASURES (RFC 7471, SECTIONS 4.5 TO 4.7)

cells: Maximum Bandwidth minus the bandwidth currently allocated to RSVP-TE LSPs. For a bundled link, the sum of the component links.
Residual bandwidth minus the measured bandwidth used for forwarding non-RSVP-TE packets. For a bundled link, the sum of the component links.
The actual utilization of the link as measured by the advertising node. For a bundled link, the sum of the component links.

viz.caption: THE RULES FOR WHEN A NEW VALUE IS ADVERTISED (RFC 7471, SECTION 5)

items.title: Average first
items.text: Every value except min/max delay and residual bandwidth must be an average over a period, or a filter that stands in for one.

items.title: Advertise at once
items.text: The advertisement is made immediately when the value leaves its bound, or when the change since the last advertised value exceeds a threshold.

items.title: Raise and clear the alarm
items.text: For the sub-TLVs with an A bit, an extra threshold marks the point at which performance counts as anomalous. The bit clears once the value stays below it for an advertisement interval.

items.title: One threshold only
items.text: To prevent oscillations, only the high threshold or the low threshold, but not both, may trigger a given sub-TLV.
